symptoms: Olive-green to black velvety spots on leaf surfaces and fruit
Leaves become distorted, puckered, and drop prematurely
Scabby, corky brown lesions on fruit surface
causes: Ascomycete fungus overwintering in fallen dead leaves
favorable_conditions: Cool, wet spring weather (15-24°C) with prolonged leaf wetness (>9 hours)
prevention: Collect and destroy fallen leaf litter in autumn to reduce primary inoculum
Prune apple canopy to allow maximum sunlight penetration and rapid leaf drying
Plant scab-resistant cultivars such as Prima, Priscilla, or Co-op selections
cultural_control: Apply 5% urea spray on foliage just before leaf fall to accelerate decomposition of scab fungus in leaves
Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation that keeps leaves wet
biological_control: Foliar application of Bacillus subtilis or Trichoderma harzianum formulations at bud break
Bio-fungicidal sulfur or potassium bicarbonate sprays in organic orchards
chemical_control: Preventive foliar spray of Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L of water at silver tip to green tip stage
Curative foliar spray of Difenoconazole 25% EC @ 0.3 ml/L or Captan 50% WP @ 2.0 g/L at petal fall stage
Note: Rotate chemical groups to prevent fungal fungicide resistance
treatment_notes: Follow CIBRC approved label dosages and local State Horticulture Department / KVK advisories. Observe 14-21 days pre-harvest interval (PHI).
severity_guidance: High risk during flowering and fruit set. Immediate spray needed if leaf wetness exceeds 10 hours during spring.
sources: ICAR-CITH Srinagar (Central Institute of Temperate Horticulture)
Dr. YSP UHF Nauni Apple Disease Advisory

symptoms: Small purple specks enlarging into circular 'frogeye' spots with tan centers and dark purple borders
Black, rotting fruit with concentric rings, eventually mummifying on tree
Bark cankers on branches and trunk
causes: Fungal pathogen entering through wounds, fire blight strikes, or winter injuries
favorable_conditions: Warm, humid weather (20-28°C) with frequent rain
prevention: Prune out dead wood, fire blight cankers, and remove mummified apples from the orchard
Maintain tree vigor through balanced fertilization and irrigation
cultural_control: Burn or bury pruned diseased wood immediately
biological_control: Trichoderma viride spray on pruning cuts to prevent fungal colonization
chemical_control: Spray Captan 50% WP @ 2.0 g/L or Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L from pink bud through cover sprays
Thiophanate Methyl 70% WP @ 1.0 g/L for canker management
treatment_notes: Follow product label directions and local KVK advisory.
severity_guidance: Moderate to high in neglected orchards.

symptoms: Bright yellow-orange spots on upper leaf surfaces
Tiny tube-like fungal aecia structures forming on the underside of leaves and fruit
Early defoliation and fruit distortion
causes: Heteroecious rust fungus requiring both apple and juniper/cedar trees to complete life cycle
favorable_conditions: Wet spring conditions when galls on nearby junipers produce gelatinous spore horns
prevention: Remove Eastern red cedar and juniper trees within a 1-2 km radius of the orchard if feasible
Plant rust-immune varieties such as Liberty or Enterprise
cultural_control: Prune out cedar galls from nearby ornamental junipers before spring rains
biological_control: Neem-based formulations and Bacillus subtilis as preventive sprays
chemical_control: Foliar spray of Myclobutanil 10% WP @ 0.5 g/L or Trifloxystrobin + Tebuconazole @ 0.5 g/L from tight cluster to petal fall
treatment_notes: Spray must be applied preventively as spores land from cedar galls.
severity_guidance: Moderate economic impact, mainly cosmetic unless severe defoliation occurs.

symptoms: Vigorous green foliage with no discoloration, spots, mildew, or lesions
causes: Normal physiological health
favorable_conditions: Balanced soil nutrition, adequate chilling hours, proper sunlight, and integrated pest management
prevention: Continue balanced N-P-K and micronutrient (Boron, Zinc, Calcium) fertilization based on annual soil tests
Maintain regular pruning and drip irrigation schedules
cultural_control: Weed clearing around tree basins and annual winter pruning
biological_control: Maintain beneficial predator insects (ladybugs, predatory mites) by avoiding broad-spectrum insecticides
chemical_control: No chemical treatment needed.
treatment_notes: Plant is completely healthy. No chemical intervention required.
severity_guidance: Zero risk.
sources: ICAR Package of Practices for Temperate Fruits

symptoms: Small, tan spots with yellow halos that elongate into narrow, rectangular lesions bounded by leaf veins
Lesions turn grayish as fungus sporulates, merging to scorch entire leaves
causes: Airborne and crop residue-borne fungal pathogen
favorable_conditions: Warm, humid conditions (>25°C, >90% RH) common in continuous maize cropping under minimum tillage
prevention: Practice 1-2 year crop rotation with non-host crops like soybean, pulses, or mustard
Deep plow maize stubble after harvest to bury infected residue
Use resistant maize hybrids recommended by ICAR-IIMR
cultural_control: Avoid excessive plant density to ensure good canopy air movement
biological_control: Seed treatment with Trichoderma viride @ 4 g/kg seed before sowing
chemical_control: Foliar spray of Azoxystrobin 18.2% + Difenoconazole 11.4% SC @ 1 ml/L or Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L at first symptom onset
treatment_notes: Apply spray before tasseling/silking stage if lesions reach the third leaf below the ear.
severity_guidance: High yield loss potential (20-50%) if leaf blighting occurs before grain fill.
sources: ICAR-IIMR Ludhiana (Indian Institute of Maize Research)

symptoms: Oval to elongate cinnamon-brown pustules (uredinia) scattered over both upper and lower leaf surfaces
Pustules rupture the epidermis and release powdery brown spores, later turning brownish-black
causes: Wind-borne fungal rust spores traveling long distances
favorable_conditions: Cool to moderate temperatures (16-25°C) with high relative humidity (>95%) and night dew
prevention: Sow certified rust-tolerant maize hybrids
Plant early in the season to escape late rust build-up
cultural_control: Maintain balanced nitrogen application; avoid excess vegetative flush
biological_control: Foliar application of Pseudomonas fluorescens @ 5 g/L
chemical_control: Foliar spray of Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Propiconazole 25% EC @ 1 ml/L at first appearance of pustules
treatment_notes: Spray is economically justified only when rust pustules appear on leaves below the ear before silking.
severity_guidance: Moderate in Kharif season, can be severe in Rabi/Spring maize.

Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight.disease: Northern Corn Leaf Blight (Turcicum Leaf Blight)
symptoms: Long, elliptical, cigar-shaped grayish-green to tan lesions (2.5 to 15 cm long)
Dark olive to black velvety fungal sporulation on lesions during humid weather
Leaves become blighted and appear scorched
causes: Fungus surviving on infected crop residue and seed
favorable_conditions: Moderate temperatures (18-27°C) with heavy dews and frequent rains
prevention: Select resistant maize hybrids (e.g. HQPM-1, PMH-1)
Destroy or bury crop residues after harvest
Seed treatment with Thiram 75% WP @ 2.5 g/kg seed
cultural_control: Crop rotation with non-cereal crops for at least 1 year
biological_control: Seed treatment and soil enrichment with Trichoderma harzianum @ 10 g/kg seed / 2.5 kg/ha in FYM
chemical_control: Foliar spray of Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Zineb 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L or Azoxystrobin 23% SC @ 1 ml/L at knee-high stage and repeat after 10-15 days if needed
treatment_notes: Ensure thorough coverage of middle and lower canopy leaves where infection starts.
severity_guidance: Severe yield reduction (up to 40-70%) if infection reaches ear leaf prior to silking.

symptoms: Broad, deep green leaves with clean venation and sturdy stalk
causes: Optimal soil nutrients, moisture, and pest-free environment
favorable_conditions: Adequate warmth (25-32°C), fertile well-drained loamy soil, and timely irrigation at knee-high, tasseling, and grain-filling stages
prevention: Apply split nitrogen doses (1/3 at basal, 1/3 at knee-high, 1/3 at tasseling)
Monitor fields regularly for Fall Armyworm (Spodoptera frugiperda) traps
cultural_control: Intercropping with cowpea or pulses to suppress weeds and improve nitrogen balance
biological_control: Install pheromone traps @ 5 traps/acre for pest monitoring
chemical_control: No chemical treatment needed.
treatment_notes: Plant is vigorous and healthy. Maintain standard nutrient and irrigation schedule.
severity_guidance: Zero risk.
sources: ICAR Package of Practices for Maize

Cotton___Bacterial_Blight.disease: Bacterial Blight / Angular Leaf Spot / Black Arm
symptoms: Water-soaked, angular spots on leaves bounded by veins, turning dark brown to black
Black lesions on petioles and stems causing 'Black Arm' phase, leading to stem breakage
Round, water-soaked dark sunken spots on bolls causing premature boll rotting and fiber staining
causes: Seed-borne and debris-borne bacterial pathogen entering through stomata or wounds
favorable_conditions: Warm, humid weather (28-35°C, >85% RH) with driving rains and sprinkler irrigation
prevention: Use certified, acid-delinted seeds treated with concentrated sulfuric acid
Seed soaking in Streptocycline solution (100 ppm) for 2 hours before sowing
Grow tolerant/resistant cotton hybrids recommended by ICAR-CICR
Burn or deep plow previous season cotton stubble
cultural_control: Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which promotes dense, succulent vegetative growth susceptible to bacterial spread
Adopt wider spacing to promote canopy ventilation and fast drying of foliage
biological_control: Seed bio-priming with Pseudomonas fluorescens @ 10 g/kg seed
Foliar spray of P. fluorescens (0.2%) at 30, 45, and 60 days after sowing
chemical_control: Foliar spray of Copper Oxychloride 50% WP @ 2.5–3.0 g/L PLUS Streptocycline @ 0.1–0.2 g/L (1-2 g per 10 L water) at first symptom appearance
Repeat spray at 12-15 day intervals depending on rain frequency
treatment_notes: Sourced from ICAR-CICR Cotton Protection Guidelines. Always combine copper oxychloride with streptocycline for synergistic bacterial control. Follow CIBRC approved label dosages.
severity_guidance: High economic threat in rainfed and irrigated cotton belts of Gujarat, Maharashtra, Punjab, and Telangana. Stem breakage causes total loss.
sources: ICAR-CICR Nagpur (Central Institute for Cotton Research)

symptoms: Upward or downward curling and thickening of leaf margins
Thickening of small veins (vein clearing and darkening) on the undersurface of leaves
Leaf-like enations (outgrowths) on the main veins beneath the leaf
Stunted bushy plant growth with reduced boll formation
causes: Geminivirus transmitted exclusively by the whitefly vector (Bemisia tabaci)
favorable_conditions: High temperatures (30-40°C), dry spells, and heavy whitefly vector population in North and Central cotton zones
prevention: Eradicate weed hosts (Abutilon indicum, Sida cordifolia, Parthenium) around field borders
Sow CLCuV-resistant Bt-cotton hybrids recommended by PAU/CCSHAU/ICAR-CICR
Avoid growing alternative whitefly hosts like brinjal, okra, or sunflower adjacent to cotton
cultural_control: Install yellow sticky traps @ 15-20 traps/acre at crop canopy level for early whitefly mass-trapping
Uproot and bury severely virus-infected plants during early vegetative stage (<45 DAS)
biological_control: Foliar spray of 5% Neem Seed Kernel Extract (NSKE) or Neem oil 1500 ppm @ 5 ml/L at early vegetative stage
Conserve natural whitefly predators like Chrysoperla carnea and Encarsia parasitoids
chemical_control: Chemical control targets the whitefly insect vector (viruses cannot be killed directly by chemical sprays):
Spray Diafenthiuron 50% WP @ 1.2 g/L or Afidopyropen 50 g/L DC @ 2 ml/L or Pyriproxyfen 10% EC @ 2 ml/L
Alternate with Flonicamid 50% WG @ 0.3 g/L or Dinotefuran 20% SG @ 0.3 g/L to avoid vector insecticide resistance
treatment_notes: Sourced from ICAR-CICR and PAU Ludhiana advisories. Chemical sprays target the insect vector (Whitefly) only; there is no chemical cure for the plant once systemic virus infection occurs.
severity_guidance: Devastating in Northwest India (Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan). Early infection can cause 50-80% yield loss.

symptoms: Yellowing and browning of cotyledons and lower leaves, starting from leaf margins
Leaves wilt, wither, and drop, leaving a bare stem with small tufts of leaves at top
Dark brown to black vascular discoloration in the stem when split longitudinally
causes: Soil-borne fungus surviving in soil for many years as chlamydospores
favorable_conditions: Acidic to neutral soils, soil temperatures of 25-32°C, and presence of root-knot nematodes
prevention: Use wilt-immune or tolerant cotton cultivars (Desi cottons are generally more resistant than American cottons)
Treat seeds with Trichoderma viride @ 4 g/kg seed or Carbendazim 50% WP @ 2 g/kg seed before sowing
cultural_control: Long crop rotation (3-5 years) with non-host crops such as sorghum, maize, or bajra
Apply enriched farmyard manure with Trichoderma bio-agent to suppress soil pathogen load
biological_control: Soil application of Trichoderma viride / T. harzianum @ 2.5 kg mixed in 250 kg FYM per acre at the time of field preparation
Application of neem cake @ 150 kg/acre
chemical_control: Spot drenching around wilted plants with Carbendazim 50% WP @ 1 g/L or Copper Oxychloride 50% WP @ 3 g/L to contain localized spread
treatment_notes: Soil-borne disease. Soil drenching and bio-control enrichment are the primary defense lines.
severity_guidance: Can cause 30-60% plant mortality in susceptible cotton cultivars on infested soils.

symptoms: Lush green palmate leaves with healthy vegetative nodes, clean squares, and developing bolls
causes: Optimal soil fertility, balanced nutrition, and effective pest management
favorable_conditions: Warm sunny climate (25-35°C), deep black soil (Vertisol) or alluvial loam, adequate moisture without waterlogging
prevention: Apply recommended NPK doses (e.g. 120:60:60 kg/ha) with split nitrogen applications
Foliar spray of 1% Magnesium Sulfate + 1% Potassium Nitrate (13:0:45) at flowering and boll development to prevent leaf reddening
cultural_control: Regular weeding, earthing up at 45 DAS, and monitoring with pheromone traps for pink bollworm
biological_control: Install pheromone traps @ 2 traps/acre for pink bollworm (Pectinophora gossypiella) monitoring
chemical_control: No chemical treatment needed.
treatment_notes: Plant is completely healthy. Continue standard agronomic and irrigation practices.
severity_guidance: Zero risk.
sources: ICAR-CICR Package of Practices for Cotton

symptoms: Small, circular reddish-brown leaf spots with tiny black dots (pycnidia) arranged in a ring
Berries develop light brown sunken spots, quickly rot, turn black, shrivel into hard, wrinkled mummies
causes: Overwintering fungal perithecia and pycnidia in mummified berries and cane lesions
favorable_conditions: Warm, wet weather (21-32°C) with frequent showers during early berry development
prevention: Prune and destroy all mummified berries on vines and ground during winter dormancy
Canopy management to ensure air circulation and rapid bunch drying
cultural_control: Remove suckers and thin leaves around grape clusters
biological_control: Bacillus subtilis bio-fungicide spray at 10-day intervals
chemical_control: Spray Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Myclobutanil 10% WP @ 0.5 g/L or Azoxystrobin 23% SC @ 1 ml/L from bud break through veraison
treatment_notes: Protect berries from flowering stage through 4-5 weeks post-bloom when berries are most susceptible.
severity_guidance: Can cause 100% crop loss in humid grape growing regions if uncontrolled.
sources: ICAR-NRCG Pune (National Research Centre for Grapes)

symptoms: 'Tiger-stripe' leaf pattern: chlorotic and necrotic areas between veins with green borders
Dark brown to purple spots ('measles') on berry skin, berry cracking and drying
Internal dark brown to black wood streaking and soft yellow spongy wood rot
causes: Complex of fungal wood-decay pathogens entering through large pruning wounds
favorable_conditions: Mature vineyards (>8-10 years old), stressed vines, and frequent rainy winter pruning periods
prevention: Prune during dry weather and immediately paint large cuts (>2 cm) with fungal wound sealant or copper paste
Sterilize pruning shears between vines with 70% alcohol or 10% bleach solution
cultural_control: Uproot and burn severely decayed vines showing apoplexy (sudden vine collapse)
biological_control: Apply Trichoderma atroviride / T. harzianum paste on pruning wounds within 24 hours of cutting
chemical_control: Apply Thiophanate-methyl 70% WP + Copper Oxychloride paste on thick pruning cuts to prevent wood pathogen entry
treatment_notes: No curative chemical spray exists for systemic trunk rot. Prevention and wound protection are vital.
severity_guidance: Chronic disease reducing vineyard productive lifespan by 30-50%.

symptoms: Irregular brown to dark necrotic spots on leaves with distinct yellowish margins
Spots coalesce into large dead leaf patches, causing premature defoliation before harvest
Affected vines fail to ripen cane wood properly
causes: Airborne fungal conidia flourishing in late summer and post-monsoon
favorable_conditions: Humid post-monsoon weather (24-30°C) with morning dew and intermittent showers
prevention: Collect and burn fallen leaves after harvest
Avoid overhead irrigation and maintain open vine canopy
cultural_control: Post-harvest shoot trimming to enhance airflow
biological_control: Pseudomonas fluorescens foliar spray @ 5 g/L
chemical_control: Foliar spray of Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Chlorothalonil 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L or Azoxystrobin 23% SC @ 1 ml/L
treatment_notes: Spray immediately after monsoon showers to prevent premature leaf drop before cane maturation.
severity_guidance: Moderate, causes poor cane maturity and lower bud fruitfulness in the following season.

symptoms: Uniform green leaves without spots, strong tendrils, and clean berry bunches
causes: Good vineyard management, balanced fertigation, and disease monitoring
favorable_conditions: Warm dry days (28-35°C), cool nights, well-drained loamy soil (pH 6.5-7.5), and drip fertigation
prevention: Fertigate with balanced NPK + Calcium/Magnesium according to phenological stage
Perform shoot positioning and cluster thinning at bunch pea-size stage
cultural_control: Regular summer pruning and sub-cane training
biological_control: Maintain native predatory thrips and spider mite predators by avoiding broad-spectrum insecticides
chemical_control: No chemical treatment needed.
treatment_notes: Vineyard is healthy. Follow standard crop canopy and fertigation schedule.
severity_guidance: Zero risk.

symptoms: Small, dark brown to black circular spots on older lower leaves with characteristic concentric rings ('target-board' pattern)
Yellowing of leaf tissue surrounding lesions; severe infection causes leaf drop and reduced tuber sizing
Dark, sunken, dry circular lesions on potato tubers
causes: Soil-borne and crop residue-borne fungal pathogen
favorable_conditions: Warm temperatures (24-30°C) with alternating wet periods (rain, dew, sprinkler irrigation) and dry sunny spells
prevention: Plant certified disease-free seed tubers
Practice 2-3 year crop rotation with non-solanaceous crops (e.g. maize, legumes, wheat)
Maintain adequate soil nitrogen and potassium nutrition to prevent premature crop senescence
cultural_control: Destroy crop residues immediately after harvest; avoid sprinkler irrigation late in the evening
biological_control: Foliar spray of Trichoderma harzianum @ 5 g/L or Bacillus subtilis @ 5 g/L at early vegetative stage
chemical_control: Preventive spray of Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Chlorothalonil 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L at 45 days after planting
Curative spray of Azoxystrobin 18.2% + Difenoconazole 11.4% SC @ 1 ml/L or Tebuconazole 25.9% EC @ 1 ml/L upon initial lesion detection
treatment_notes: Spray must cover lower canopy leaves thoroughly. Observe 14 days pre-harvest interval (PHI).
severity_guidance: Moderate to high, causes 15-35% tuber yield reduction if foliage blights early.

symptoms: Water-soaked, irregular pale green to dark brown lesions on leaves, expanding rapidly
Delicate white cottony fungal growth on the underside of infected leaves in humid conditions
Entire foliage collapses and rots within days, emitting a foul decaying odor
Tubers show shallow, irregular, purplish-brown dry rot extending into flesh
causes: Oomycete pathogen surviving in infected seed tubers, volunteer potato plants, and cull piles
favorable_conditions: Cool, moist weather (12-22°C) with continuous high humidity (>90% RH) and frequent rain or dense fog
prevention: Plant late-blight resistant potato varieties (e.g. Kufri Girdhari, Kufri Himalini, Kufri Mohan, Kufri Jyoti)
Use certified, inspected seed tubers; destroy volunteer plants and cull dumps before planting
Earth up potato ridges well to prevent fungal sporangia from washing down to tubers
cultural_control: Dehaulm (cut foliage) 10-12 days before harvest to prevent tuber contamination during lifting
biological_control: Foliar spray of Trichoderma viride enriched formulation as preventive measure
chemical_control: Preventive spray: Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Copper Oxychloride 50% WP @ 3.0 g/L at canopy closure
Curative spray: Cymoxanil 8% + Mancozeb 64% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Metalaxyl 8% + Mancozeb 64% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Dimethomorph 50% WP @ 1.0 g/L upon first symptom alert
treatment_notes: Highly destructive. Apply systemic fungicides immediately upon CPRI/KVK blight warning alerts. Alternate chemistries to prevent Metalaxyl resistance.
severity_guidance: Extremely critical. Can destroy an entire potato field in 4-7 days if weather remains cloudy and wet.

symptoms: Vigorous green compound leaves, strong upright stems, and healthy root and stolon network
causes: Certified disease-free seed, balanced soil fertility, and proper earthing up
favorable_conditions: Cool day temperatures (18-25°C), cool night temperatures (12-16°C for tuberization), sandy loam soil rich in organic matter (pH 5.5-6.5)
prevention: Perform earthing up at 30-35 days after planting to prevent greening of tubers
Ensure balanced N-P-K (150:100:120 kg/ha) with adequate potassium for tuber bulk and disease resistance
cultural_control: Regular weeding and proper furrow irrigation without water stagnation
biological_control: Seed tuber treatment with Trichoderma viride @ 5 g/kg seed before planting
chemical_control: No chemical treatment needed.
treatment_notes: Plant is healthy. Maintain regular soil moisture and earthing up.
severity_guidance: Zero risk.
sources: ICAR-CPRI Package of Practices for Potato

symptoms: Water-soaked lesions on leaf margins, rapidly turning yellow to straw-colored with wavy edges
Milky bacterial exudate droplets oozing from lesions in early morning, drying into yellow crusts
'Kresek' (seedling wilt) phase causing complete drying of seedlings
causes: Bacterial pathogen spread through irrigation water, typhoons, wind-driven rain, and infected seed
favorable_conditions: Warm temperatures (25-34°C), high humidity (>70%), heavy rainfall, and excessive nitrogen fertilization
prevention: Grow BLB-resistant rice varieties (e.g. Improved Samba Mahsuri, Swarna-Sub1 with Xa21 gene, DRR Dhan 44)
Seed treatment with Streptocycline @ 0.1 g/L + Copper Oxychloride @ 1 g/L for 8 hours before nursery sowing
Avoid clipping seedling leaf tips during transplantation
cultural_control: Apply nitrogen in 3-4 split doses; avoid excessive top-dressing during vegetative and panicle initiation stages
Drain standing water from infected fields and avoid flowing irrigation water to adjacent healthy fields
biological_control: Seed treatment and foliar spray with Pseudomonas fluorescens @ 10 g/L at 45 and 60 DAT
chemical_control: Foliar spray of Copper Oxychloride 50% WP @ 2.5 g/L PLUS Streptocycline @ 0.15 g/L (1.5 g in 10 L water)
Alternatively spray Kasugamycin 3% SL @ 2.0 ml/L or Thifluzamide 24% SC for complex infections
treatment_notes: Drain excess water from field before spraying. Sourced from ICAR-NRRI Cuttack.
severity_guidance: High yield loss potential (20-50%) in Kharif season across coastal and irrigated belts.

symptoms: Leaf Blast: Spindle-shaped or diamond-shaped lesions with grayish-white centers and dark brown borders
Neck Blast: Blackish rot at the panicle base causing the entire panicle to fall over, producing chaffy white grains ('empty panicles')
Node Blast: Blackened, fragile nodes on stem that easily break
causes: Airborne fungal conidia produced in millions on infected blast lesions
favorable_conditions: Cool night temperatures (18-24°C) with high daytime humidity (>90%), long dew periods, and excess nitrogen
prevention: Plant blast-tolerant rice cultivars (e.g. Rasi, IR-64, DRR Dhan varieties)
Seed treatment with Tricyclazole 75% WP @ 2 g/kg seed or Carbendazim 50% WP @ 2 g/kg seed
Balanced fertilizer application: Avoid excess urea; apply potash (K2O) to strengthen cell walls
cultural_control: Burn infected stubble; maintain thin nursery density to prevent humid microclimate
biological_control: Seed and foliar treatment with Pseudomonas fluorescens @ 10 g/kg seed / 5 g/L spray
chemical_control: Foliar spray of Tricyclazole 75% WP @ 0.6 g/L or Isoprothiolane 40% EC @ 1.5 ml/L or Azoxystrobin 18.2% + Difenoconazole 11.4% SC @ 1 ml/L
For Neck Blast prevention: Apply first spray at 5-10% flowering/booting stage and second spray at full panicle emergence
treatment_notes: Neck blast spray timing is critical: once neck rot sets in, chemical sprays cannot reverse grain emptiness.
severity_guidance: Severe. Neck blast can destroy 50-90% of grain yield within days.

symptoms: Numerous small, oval to circular dark brown spots with gray or whitish centers and yellow halos on leaves
Dark brown to black discoloration on glumes and grains leading to poor germination and reduced grain weight
Seedling blight resulting in yellowing and death of young rice seedlings
causes: Seed-borne and soil-borne fungal pathogen prevalent on nutrient-stressed crops
favorable_conditions: Temperatures of 25-30°C, high humidity, sandy nutrient-deficient soils lacking potassium, silicon, or zinc
prevention: Correct soil nutrient deficiencies: apply recommended NPK, Zinc Sulfate (25 kg/ha), and Potassium
Seed treatment with Carbendazim 50% WP @ 2 g/kg seed or Thiram 75% WP @ 3 g/kg seed
cultural_control: Avoid intermittent drought stress in fields; keep soil adequately moist
biological_control: Seed bio-priming with Trichoderma viride @ 5 g/kg seed
chemical_control: Foliar spray of Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Propiconazole 25% EC @ 1 ml/L or Edifenphos 50% EC @ 1 ml/L at tillering and boot leaf stage
treatment_notes: Correcting soil fertility (potash and zinc) is equally important as fungicide spraying.
severity_guidance: Moderate to high in direct-seeded rice and light soils.

symptoms: Vigorous green erect tillers, healthy white root system, and clean green leaf blades without spots
causes: Good nursery management, balanced fertigation, and proper water leveling
favorable_conditions: Warm temperatures (22-32°C), abundant sunlight, clay-loam soil with good water retention, and 2-5 cm standing water layer during vegetative growth
prevention: Apply nitrogen in 3 equal splits: basal, active tillering, and panicle initiation stage
Apply Zinc Sulfate @ 25 kg/ha at basal transplanting to prevent Khaira disease (zinc deficiency)
cultural_control: Maintain alternate wetting and drying (AWD) irrigation to save water and promote deep root aeration
biological_control: Encourage dragonflies and spiders as natural planthopper predators
chemical_control: No chemical treatment needed.
treatment_notes: Rice crop is in healthy condition. Follow recommended nitrogen top-dressing and water management.
severity_guidance: Zero risk.
sources: ICAR-NRRI Package of Practices for Rice

Tomato___Bacterial_spot.scientific_name: Xanthomonas perforans / Xanthomonas campestris pv. vesicatoria
symptoms: Small, water-soaked dark brown circular spots (1-3 mm) on leaves with yellow halos
Spots coalesce causing leaf browning, blighting, and severe defoliation
Black, raised, blister-like scabby spots on green tomato fruits
causes: Seed-borne bacterium and volunteer solanaceous weed hosts spread by splashing rain
favorable_conditions: Warm temperatures (25-32°C) with high relative humidity and overhead rainfall or sprinkler irrigation
prevention: Use certified disease-free seeds or hot water treated seeds (50°C for 25 minutes)
Practice 2-year crop rotation avoiding tomato, pepper, eggplant, and potato
Avoid working in tomato fields when foliage is wet
cultural_control: Drip irrigation instead of overhead sprinklers to keep foliage dry
biological_control: Foliar spray of Bacillus subtilis or Pseudomonas fluorescens @ 5 g/L
chemical_control: Foliar spray of Copper Oxychloride 50% WP @ 2.5 g/L PLUS Streptocycline @ 0.1 g/L (1 g in 10 L water) every 7-10 days during rainy weather
treatment_notes: Preventive copper-streptocycline sprays are essential during humid spells. Sourced from ICAR-IIHR.
severity_guidance: High risk in monsoon tomato crops; fruit lesions make produce unmarketable.
sources: ICAR-IIHR Bengaluru (Indian Institute of Horticultural Research)

symptoms: Circular dark brown to black spots on older leaves with distinct concentric rings ('target-board' effect)
Yellowing of leaf tissue surrounding spots, leading to premature leaf defoliation from bottom upward
Sunken, dark leathery lesions at the stem end of tomato fruits ('collar rot' on seedlings)
causes: Fungal pathogen surviving in soil, infected seed, and solanaceous crop debris
favorable_conditions: Warm temperatures (24-29°C) with alternating heavy dews/rains and dry periods
prevention: Stake tomato plants and mulch soil surface to prevent soil splash onto lower foliage
Prune bottom leaves (15-20 cm above ground) to improve air circulation
Practice 3-year crop rotation with non-solanaceous crops
cultural_control: Destroy infected plant debris after harvest; use drip irrigation
biological_control: Foliar application of Trichoderma viride @ 5 g/L or Pseudomonas fluorescens @ 5 g/L
chemical_control: Foliar spray of Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Chlorothalonil 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L as preventive spray
Foliar spray of Azoxystrobin 18.2% + Difenoconazole 11.4% SC @ 1 ml/L or Tebuconazole 25.9% EC @ 1 ml/L upon initial lesion detection
treatment_notes: Ensure complete coverage of lower leaves where disease begins. 7-14 day PHI.
severity_guidance: Moderate to high, causes significant sun-scald on fruits due to loss of foliage.

symptoms: Large, irregular water-soaked greenish-black lesions on leaves that rapidly turn brown and papery
White fungal downy growth on the underside of leaves and stems in humid conditions
Dark brown, firm, greasy-surfaced lesions on green tomato fruits causing total fruit rot
Rapid collapse and browning of entire vine within 3-5 days
causes: Oomycete pathogen spread rapidly by wind-blown sporangia during cool wet weather
favorable_conditions: Cool, wet weather (15-22°C) with continuous high humidity (>90% RH), morning fog, and persistent rain
prevention: Plant late-blight tolerant hybrid tomato varieties (e.g. Arka Rakshak, Arka Samrat from ICAR-IIHR with triple disease resistance)
Provide wide row spacing and stake plants to ensure rapid leaf drying
Avoid planting tomatoes adjacent to potato fields
cultural_control: Remove and bury infected tomato plants and cull fruits immediately
biological_control: Preventive foliar application of Trichoderma harzianum @ 5 g/L
chemical_control: Preventive spray: Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Copper Oxychloride 50% WP @ 3.0 g/L at first cool, humid weather forecast
Curative spray: Cymoxanil 8% + Mancozeb 64% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Metalaxyl-M 4% + Mancozeb 64% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Dimethomorph 50% WP @ 1.0 g/L upon first lesion appearance
treatment_notes: Critical disease. Spray immediately upon first symptoms or ICAR/KVK regional blight advisory. Sourced from ICAR-IIHR Bangalore.
severity_guidance: Extremely high. Can cause 100% crop loss in 5-7 days under favorable conditions.

symptoms: Pale green to yellowish spots on upper leaf surface with indefinite margins
Dense, velvety olive-green to grayish-brown fungal mold on the underside of leaves corresponding to yellow spots
Leaves turn brown, curl, and wither prematurely
causes: Fungus thriving in enclosed, humid environments with poor ventilation
favorable_conditions: High relative humidity (>85%) and moderate temperatures (20-25°C), very common in polyhouse/greenhouse tomatoes
prevention: Maintain adequate greenhouse/polyhouse ventilation and air circulation
Space plants properly and prune suckers/lower leaves to open up canopy
Use drip irrigation to keep foliage completely dry
cultural_control: Ventilate polyhouses early in the morning to reduce humidity condensation
biological_control: Foliar spray of Bacillus amyloliquefaciens or Trichoderma viride @ 5 g/L
chemical_control: Foliar spray of Chlorothalonil 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L or Azoxystrobin 23% SC @ 1 ml/L or Difenoconazole 25% EC @ 0.5 ml/L
treatment_notes: Reduce polyhouse humidity below 80% to arrest fungal sporulation.
severity_guidance: Moderate in open fields; high severity in polyhouse / protected cultivation.

symptoms: Numerous small (1.5-3 mm), circular spots with dark brown margins and gray/tan centers
Tiny black speck-like pycnidia visible inside the center of each spot
Progressive yellowing and defoliation from bottom leaves upward, leaving fruits exposed to sunscald
causes: Fungus overwintering in solanaceous crop debris and weeds (horse nettle, nightshade)
favorable_conditions: Warm temperatures (20-27°C) with prolonged wet foliage and high humidity
prevention: Stake tomato vines and mulch ground with black plastic or organic mulch
Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation and working in wet tomato fields
Practice 2-3 year crop rotation
cultural_control: Prune out lower infected leaves at first symptom detection
biological_control: Foliar spray of Pseudomonas fluorescens @ 5 g/L
chemical_control: Foliar spray of Chlorothalonil 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L or Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Azoxystrobin 23% SC @ 1 ml/L every 7-10 days
treatment_notes: Spray lower canopy thoroughly at first sign of circular spots.
severity_guidance: Moderate to high, causes extensive defoliation and severe fruit sunscald.

symptoms: Fine yellow to white stippling / speckling on upper leaf surface
Leaves turn bronze, dry, brittle, and drop prematurely
Fine silky webbing covering the underside of leaves, growing tips, and fruit clusters
Tiny moving reddish-brown to translucent mites visible under a hand lens on leaf undersides
causes: Polyphagous phytophagous mite reproducing rapidly in hot, dry, dusty conditions
favorable_conditions: Hot, dry weather (>30°C, <60% RH) and dusty conditions, often triggered by overuse of synthetic pyrethroid insecticides
prevention: Avoid water stress; maintain adequate soil moisture to keep plant sap flowing
Sprinkle water on field pathways to suppress dust
Avoid broad-spectrum synthetic pyrethroids (e.g. Cypermethrin) that kill natural predatory mites
cultural_control: Wash lower leaf surfaces with high-pressure water spray to dislodge mite webbing
biological_control: Spray 5% Neem Seed Kernel Extract (NSKE) or Neem Oil 10000 ppm @ 3 ml/L
Release predatory phytoseiid mites (Phytoseiulus persimilis / Neoseiulus californicus) in polyhouses
chemical_control: Foliar spray of Propargite 57% EC @ 2 ml/L or Spiromesifen 22.9% SC @ 1 ml/L or Fenpyroximate 5% EC @ 1 ml/L or Abamectin 1.9% EC @ 0.5 ml/L
Ensure spray reaches the underside of all leaves where mites reside
treatment_notes: Must spray with high pressure targeting leaf undersides. Rotate miticide chemistries to prevent resistance.
severity_guidance: High in summer open-field and greenhouse crops. Can cause complete crop bronzing in 10-14 days.

symptoms: Small, water-soaked pinpoint spots on leaves enlarging into brown lesions with light brown centers and dark concentric rings
Dark, sunken, circular lesions on tomato fruits with prominent cracked centers
Lesions on stems and petioles causing girdling
causes: Fungal pathogen with a broad host range including tomato, cotton, cucumber, and soybean
favorable_conditions: Warm, humid conditions (20-30°C) with prolonged moisture and rain
prevention: Stake and prune tomato plants to allow maximum airflow
Remove solanaceous and cucurbit weed hosts around the field
Rotate with non-host crops like corn or sorghum
cultural_control: Avoid overhead irrigation; destroy infected crop residues after harvest
biological_control: Foliar application of Bacillus subtilis @ 5 g/L
chemical_control: Foliar spray of Azoxystrobin 23% SC @ 1 ml/L or Pyraclostrobin 20% WG @ 1 g/L or Chlorothalonil 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L
treatment_notes: Apply preventive sprays in humid weather before flowering.
severity_guidance: Moderate to high, causes significant fruit lesions and market rejection.

symptoms: Severe stunting and erect, bushy growth habit of plants
Upward curling, cupping, and crinkling of leaf margins with marked chlorosis (yellowing)
Leaves are reduced in size (shoestring appearance)
Flower abortion and failure to set fruit; if infected early, total yield loss
causes: Virus transmitted exclusively by the sweetpotato whitefly (Bemisia tabaci) in a persistent manner
favorable_conditions: Hot, dry weather that promotes high whitefly vector multiplication (28-38°C)
prevention: Plant TYLCV-resistant tomato hybrids (e.g. Arka Rakshak, Arka Samrat, US-440, Lakshmi)
Cover seedling nursery beds with 40-50 mesh insect-proof nylon net to prevent early whitefly transmission
Eradicate weed hosts (Parthenium, Croton, Datura) around tomato plots
cultural_control: Install yellow sticky traps @ 20-25 traps/acre for mass whitefly trapping
Uproot and destroy virus-infected plants within 30 days of transplanting
biological_control: Spray 5% Neem Seed Kernel Extract (NSKE) or Neem Oil 1500 ppm @ 5 ml/L at weekly intervals to deter whiteflies
Conserve mirid bugs and ladybird beetles
chemical_control: Chemical sprays target the insect vector (Whitefly); no chemical cures the viral infection in the plant:
Spray Diafenthiuron 50% WP @ 1.2 g/L or Cyantraniliprole 10.26% OD @ 1.8 ml/L or Flonicamid 50% WG @ 0.3 g/L or Pyriproxyfen 10% EC @ 2 ml/L at first whitefly observation
treatment_notes: Sourced from ICAR-IIHR Bengaluru. Protect nursery seedlings with 50-mesh nylon net. Chemical sprays target the insect vector (Whitefly) only.
severity_guidance: Extremely high. Infection in first 4 weeks after transplanting results in 90-100% yield loss.

symptoms: Mottling of leaves with alternating light and dark green patches ('mosaic' pattern)
Distorted, blistered, or fern-like narrow leaves
Stunted plant growth and uneven internal browning ('brown wall') of tomato fruits
causes: Mechanically transmitted virus through tools, worker hands, clothing, seed, and tobacco residue
favorable_conditions: Easily spread by mechanical contact during pruning, tying, and harvesting at any temperature
prevention: Use certified virus-free seed or soak seeds in 10% Trisodium Phosphate (TSP) solution for 30 minutes
Wash hands with soap and water / skimmed milk (20%) before handling tomato plants
Strictly prohibit smoking/chewing tobacco near tomato fields and polyhouses
Grow ToMV-resistant tomato varieties
cultural_control: Sterilize pruning secateurs and tools in 10% household bleach or 20% skimmed milk between plants
Uproot and burn infected plants immediately
biological_control: Foliar spray of 20% skimmed milk solution as a mechanical transmission barrier during pruning operations
chemical_control: No chemical treatment exists for viral pathogens. Control is purely preventive and sanitary.
treatment_notes: Tobamovirus is extremely stable and easily spread on hands and tools. Disinfect tools continuously.
severity_guidance: High yield and quality reduction in greenhouse and staked tomato crops.

symptoms: Lush, deep green foliage, sturdy main stem, abundant flower clusters, and smooth unblemished fruits
causes: Good agronomic care, balanced fertigation, pest monitoring, and proper staking
favorable_conditions: Warm sunny days (22-28°C), moderate night temperatures (15-20°C), well-drained sandy loam soil (pH 6.0-7.0), and regular drip irrigation
prevention: Apply balanced N-P-K (120:60:60 kg/ha) with split fertigation
Apply Calcium Nitrate @ 5 g/L during fruit expansion to prevent Blossom End Rot (calcium deficiency)
Maintain staking and mulch to keep fruit off the bare soil
cultural_control: Prune lower suckers regularly and maintain clean weed-free basins
biological_control: Install yellow and blue sticky traps @ 10 traps/acre for general pest monitoring
chemical_control: No chemical treatment needed.
treatment_notes: Tomato plant is completely healthy. Continue standard irrigation and nutrient fertigation schedule.
severity_guidance: Zero risk.
sources: ICAR-IIHR Package of Practices for Tomato

symptoms: Small, round to oval bright orange-brown pustules scattered randomly on upper leaf surfaces
Pustules rupture the epidermis and shed powdery orange-brown urediniospores on clothing/fingers
Late in season, pustules turn dark brown to black as teliospores form
causes: Airborne rust urediniospores blown across Indian wheat belts from southern and sub-Himalayan foci
favorable_conditions: Moderate temperatures (15-25°C) with high relative humidity (>85%) and 6-8 hours of dew or light rain
prevention: Sow rust-resistant wheat varieties recommended by ICAR-IIWBR (e.g. DBW 187, DBW 303, HD 3226, HD 2967, PBW 824)
Timely sowing of wheat (first fortnight of November in NWPZ and NEPZ) to avoid late-season rust buildup
Balanced NPK fertilization; avoid excessive nitrogen doses (>150 kg/ha)
cultural_control: Eradicate volunteer self-sown wheat plants during off-season
biological_control: Foliar spray of Pseudomonas fluorescens @ 5 g/L
chemical_control: Foliar spray of Propiconazole 25% EC @ 1.0 ml/L (200 ml in 200 L water per acre) or Tebuconazole 25.9% EC @ 1.0 ml/L at first appearance of brown pustules
Repeat spray after 15 days if rust progression continues
treatment_notes: Sourced from ICAR-IIWBR Karnal Wheat Protection Bulletins. One timely spray of Propiconazole 25% EC completely arrests leaf rust.
severity_guidance: High yield loss potential (15-30%) across Indo-Gangetic plains if flag leaf is infected before grain filling.
sources: ICAR-IIWBR Karnal (Indian Institute of Wheat & Barley Research)

symptoms: Bright lemon-yellow powdery pustules arranged in distinct, continuous parallel stripes along leaf veins
Yellow stripes form on leaves, leaf sheaths, and glumes
Leaves dry up and turn brown, appearing scorched, with yellow powder dusting hands and clothes
causes: Airborne fungal rust spores originating from sub-mountainous foothills (foothills of Himalayas)
favorable_conditions: Cool, humid weather (10-18°C) with frequent winter rains, morning fog, and heavy dew in North-Western Plains (Punjab, Haryana, Tarai, HP, J&K)
prevention: Grow stripe-rust resistant wheat varieties (e.g. DBW 187 [Karan Vandana], DBW 303 [Karan Vaishnavi], HD 3086, PBW 725, HD 3226)
Avoid growing susceptible older varieties like HD 2967 in rust-prone sub-mountainous areas
Regular early-morning field scouting in December-February
cultural_control: Timely sowing in November to ensure strong crop stand before January rust wave
biological_control: Foliar spray of Bacillus subtilis or bio-fungicide formulations at early vegetative stage
chemical_control: Foliar spray of Propiconazole 25% EC @ 1.0 ml/L (200 ml/acre in 200 L water) or Tebuconazole 25.9% EC @ 1.0 ml/L immediately on first detection of yellow stripes in field foci
Ensure spray reaches the whole canopy uniformly
treatment_notes: Extremely urgent. Stripe rust spreads explosively in cool fog. Spray immediately within 24-48 hours of detection. Sourced from ICAR-IIWBR Karnal.
severity_guidance: Extremely critical in Northern India. Can cause 40-80% grain shriveling and yield collapse if flag leaf is infected.

symptoms: Erect, dark green leaves without pustules, strong tillers, and healthy developing spikes (ears)
causes: Certified seed, timely sowing, balanced NPKZn nutrition, and weed management
favorable_conditions: Cool winter climate (12-22°C), fertile well-drained loam or clay-loam soil, and timely irrigation at Crown Root Initiation (CRI), tillering, jointing, flowering, and milking stages
prevention: Apply nitrogen in 3 splits (1/2 basal + 1/4 at CRI + 1/4 at second irrigation)
Apply Zinc Sulfate @ 25 kg/ha at sowing if soil test shows zinc deficiency
Ensure timely irrigation at the critical Crown Root Initiation (CRI) stage (21 days after sowing)
cultural_control: Keep field borders clean of weed grasses (Phalaris minor / Mandusi)
biological_control: Conserve natural aphid predators like coccinellid ladybird beetles
chemical_control: No chemical treatment needed.
treatment_notes: Wheat crop is healthy and vigorous. Maintain critical stage irrigation schedule.
severity_guidance: Zero risk.
sources: ICAR-IIWBR Package of Practices for Wheat

symptoms: Vigorous green foliage with no visible chlorosis, spotting, or dieback.
causes: Normal physiological condition.
favorable_conditions: Acidic soil (pH 4.5-5.5) with well-drained organic matter.
prevention: Maintain acidic soil conditions with sulfur and balanced ericaceous fertilizers.
cultural_control: Mulch with pine bark or acidic compost; drip irrigation.
biological_control: Preserve mycorrhizal root associations.
chemical_control: No chemical treatment required.
treatment_notes: Plant is healthy. Regular monitoring recommended.
severity_guidance: Zero risk.

symptoms: White powdery fungal patches on young leaves and fruit stems
Leaf curling, distortion, and premature defoliation
Web-like fungal growth on ripening cherry fruit
causes: Ascomycete fungus overwintering in bud scales and bark crevices
favorable_conditions: Warm (15-28°C), dry weather with high relative humidity and dense tree canopies
prevention: Prune inner canopy branches to promote airflow and sunlight exposure
Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization which produces susceptible tender shoot growth
cultural_control: Prune and destroy infected terminal shoots early in spring
biological_control: Foliar spray of Ampelomyces quisqualis or Potassium Bicarbonate @ 3 g/L
chemical_control: Wettable Sulfur 80% WP @ 2.5 g/L applied at shuck split and repeated at 14-day intervals
Myclobutanil 10% WP @ 1.0 g/L or Hexaconazole 5% SC @ 1.0 ml/L for curative intervention
treatment_notes: Do not apply sulfur when temperatures exceed 30°C to prevent phytotoxicity. Follow CIBRC guidelines.
severity_guidance: Moderate to high risk in young orchards and fruit development stages.

symptoms: Uniform green leaves without powdery coating, necrosis, or shot-hole lesions.
causes: Normal physiological condition.
favorable_conditions: Adequate winter chill hours and well-drained loam soil.
prevention: Regular sanitation and balanced fertilization.
cultural_control: Maintain annual dormant pruning and orchard floor clean.
biological_control: Preserve beneficial predatory mites and ladybugs.
chemical_control: No chemical treatment required.
treatment_notes: Plant is healthy. No intervention required.
severity_guidance: Zero risk.

symptoms: Blotchy mottle chlorosis on leaves with asymmetrical yellowing across midrib
Stunted, yellow upright shoots ('yellow shoots')
Small, lopsided fruit with bitter taste and aborted seeds
Severe twig dieback and gradual tree decline
causes: Phloem-limited fastidious bacterium transmitted by the Asian citrus psyllid (Diaphorina citri)
favorable_conditions: Warm subtropical climates (20-32°C) facilitating rapid vector proliferation
prevention: Plant only certified disease-free budwood from registered nurseries
Establish windbreaks to deter psyllid flights into citrus blocks
Regular scout monitoring of psyllid nymphs on new flush growth
cultural_control: Eradicate severely infected trees showing full canopy decline to prevent vector acquisition
Enhanced nutritional programs (foliar zinc, manganese, iron, potassium) to maintain tree vigor
biological_control: Release parasitoid wasps (Tamarixia radiata) for biological suppression of citrus psyllid
Apply Neem seed kernel extract (NSKE 5%) or Entomopathogenic fungi (Beauveria bassiana)
chemical_control: Vector control: Imidacloprid 17.8% SL @ 0.5 ml/L or Thiamethoxam 25% WG @ 0.3 g/L during new leaf flushes
Systemic vector rotation: Dimethoate 30% EC @ 1.5 ml/L or Chlorpyrifos 20% EC @ 2.0 ml/L
treatment_notes: Bacterial pathogen cannot be cured once systemic; rigorous vector control is mandatory. Follow ICAR-CCRI Nagpur guidelines.
severity_guidance: Critical severe risk. Threatens complete orchard longevity if vector is uncontrolled.

symptoms: Water-soaked polygonal angular spots on leaves turning purple-brown and dropping out ('shot hole')
Deep, pitted, gummy necrotic cracks on peach fruit surface
Spring and summer cankers on twigs and young branches
causes: Bacterial pathogen entering through stomata, leaf scars, and fruit lenticels
favorable_conditions: Warm (20-30°C), windy, wet spring weather with blowing rain and sandy soils
prevention: Plant tolerant varieties (e.g. Redhaven, Harvester)
Plant windbreaks to minimize blowing sand injury on tender leaves and fruit
cultural_control: Avoid excessive nitrogen that induces tender late-season succulent growth
biological_control: Bacillus amyloliquefaciens or Copper bio-complexes during early season
chemical_control: Copper Oxychloride 50% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Bordeaux mixture (1%) at late dormant / bud swell stage
Oxytetracycline / Streptocycline @ 0.5 g/L combined with Copper sprays at petal fall
treatment_notes: Do not apply high rate copper post-bloom to avoid phytotoxicity on peach leaves. Follow KVK advisory.
severity_guidance: High risk during spring wet spells.

symptoms: Lush green lanceolate leaves free from lesions, shot-hole perforations, and gumming.
causes: Normal physiological condition.
favorable_conditions: Well-drained sandy loam soil with full sunlight exposure.
prevention: Regular annual dormant spraying and balanced potassium fertilization.
cultural_control: Annual fruit thinning and canopy pruning.
biological_control: Preserve predatory wasps and hoverflies.
chemical_control: No chemical treatment required.
treatment_notes: Plant is healthy. Regular monitoring recommended.
severity_guidance: Zero risk.

symptoms: Small water-soaked circular to irregular dark green spots on leaf undersides
Lesions turn brown with greasy appearance and yellow halo, causing extensive leaf drop
Raised, warty, brown blister-like rough spots on bell pepper fruit
causes: Seed-borne and debris-borne bacterial pathogen splashing onto foliage
favorable_conditions: Warm (24-30°C) temperatures with frequent rains and high relative humidity (>85%)
prevention: Use certified disease-free treated hybrid seeds (hot water treatment at 50°C for 25 mins)
Adopt 2 to 3-year crop rotation with non-solanaceous crops (e.g. Corn, Pulses)
cultural_control: Use drip irrigation under plastic mulch; avoid overhead sprinkler watering
Disinfect pruning knives and farm equipment with 1% sodium hypochlorite solution
biological_control: Seed and seedling dip with Pseudomonas fluorescens @ 10 g/L or Bacillus subtilis @ 5 g/L
Foliar spray of organic copper bio-formulations or neem formulation (1500 ppm @ 3 ml/L)
chemical_control: Foliar spray of Copper Hydroxide 53.8% DF @ 2.0 g/L or Copper Oxychloride 50% WP @ 2.5 g/L
Combined tank-mix of Copper Oxychloride (2.0 g/L) + Streptocycline @ 0.1 g/L at early disease onset
treatment_notes: Spray during cool morning or evening hours. Comply with 7-day PHI. Follow CIBRC guidelines.
severity_guidance: High risk in monsoon/rainy season. Rapid defoliation leads to severe fruit sunscald.

symptoms: Deep green glossy leaves with robust flowering and fruit set without spots or distortion.
causes: Normal physiological condition.
favorable_conditions: Moderate temperature (20-28°C) with fertile well-drained loam.
prevention: Maintain balanced NPK fertilization and uniform soil moisture.
cultural_control: Mulching and stake support for heavy fruiting.
biological_control: Encourage beneficial biocontrol agents like Trichogramma.
chemical_control: No chemical treatment required.
treatment_notes: Plant is healthy. Regular monitoring recommended.
severity_guidance: Zero risk.

symptoms: Vigorous canes with uniform green trifoliate leaves and healthy cane growth.
causes: Normal physiological condition.
favorable_conditions: Cool temperate climate with rich organic soil.
prevention: Annual pruning of spent floricanes and trellis support.
cultural_control: Maintain 10-15 cm organic mulch.
biological_control: Preserve pollinators and beneficial predatory insects.
chemical_control: No chemical treatment required.
treatment_notes: Plant is healthy. No intervention required.
severity_guidance: Zero risk.

symptoms: Vibrant green trifoliate leaves, strong nodulation, and healthy pod development.
causes: Normal physiological condition.
favorable_conditions: Warm soil (20-30°C) with adequate monsoon moisture.
prevention: Inoculate seeds with Bradyrhizobium japonicum before sowing.
cultural_control: Maintain broad bed furrow (BBF) planting for drainage.
biological_control: Conserve natural field predators.
chemical_control: No chemical treatment required.
treatment_notes: Crop is healthy. Regular scouting recommended.
severity_guidance: Zero risk.
sources: ICAR-IISR Indore (Indian Institute of Soybean Research)

symptoms: White talcum-like powdery fungal growth on both upper and lower leaf surfaces
Infected leaves turn chlorotic, become brittle, brown, and die prematurely
Reduced fruit yield and fruit sunscald due to loss of protective leaf canopy
causes: Obligate biotrophic fungus dispersing airborne conidia across cucurbit fields
favorable_conditions: Warm dry weather (20-30°C) with shaded conditions and high relative humidity
prevention: Plant powdery mildew-resistant squash hybrids
Provide ample vine spacing (1.5 - 2.0 m) for sunlight penetration and air movement
cultural_control: Remove and bury senescing lower canopy leaves showing initial white spots
biological_control: Foliar spray of Ampelomyces quisqualis @ 5 g/L or Trichoderma viride @ 5 g/L
Baking soda (Potassium/Sodium bicarbonate @ 3 g/L) + horticultural oil (5 ml/L)
chemical_control: Wettable Sulfur 80% WDG @ 2.0 g/L (avoid in hot weather above 32°C)
Systemic spray: Azoxystrobin 18.2% + Difenoconazole 11.4% SC @ 1.0 ml/L or Hexaconazole 5% SC @ 1.0 ml/L
treatment_notes: Alternate systemic fungicides with contact sulfur to prevent resistance. Follow CIBRC guidelines.
severity_guidance: Moderate to high risk during mid-to-late fruiting period.

symptoms: Numerous small, irregular purple to dark red spots on upper leaf surfaces
Spots enlarge and merge, giving entire leaf a dry, scorched, burnt brown appearance
Leaf margins curl upward and die; calyx infection causes brown caps on fruit
causes: Ascomycete fungus surviving in infected crown leaves and plant debris
favorable_conditions: Warm, humid conditions (20-28°C) with prolonged leaf wetness
prevention: Use certified disease-free strawberry runners from tissue culture
Plant in well-drained raised beds with plastic mulch
cultural_control: Prune and destroy all older diseased foliage at renovation post-harvest
Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation; employ drip lines beneath mulch
biological_control: Foliar bio-fungicide spray of Bacillus subtilis or Trichoderma harzianum @ 5 g/L
chemical_control: Spray Captan 50% WP @ 2.0 g/L or Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L at first appearance of purple spots
Azoxystrobin 23% SC @ 1.0 ml/L or Pyraclostrobin 20% WG @ 1.0 g/L for curative control
treatment_notes: Observe 3-day pre-harvest interval for strawberry fruit. Follow KVK advisory.
severity_guidance: Moderate risk. Defoliation reduces next season crown vigor.

symptoms: Vibrant dark green trifoliate leaves, robust crowns, and clear white blossoms.
causes: Normal physiological condition.
favorable_conditions: Raised bed with drip fertigation and silver-black mulch.
prevention: Balanced fertigation with potassium and calcium during fruit sizing.
cultural_control: Maintain drip irrigation and sanitize bed runners.
biological_control: Preserve pollinating bees and beneficial predatory mites.
chemical_control: No chemical treatment required.
treatment_notes: Plant is healthy. Regular monitoring recommended.
severity_guidance: Zero risk.
